explanations.explanation: Almost, friend, but verse 2 sets the record straight. It says “…it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples.” So the disciples were doing the dunking while Jesus kept gaining followers. Thanks for taking the swing, baker.

That's right, baker. John 4:2 says it was not Jesus who baptized, but His disciples. The Pharisees heard about the crowds, but Jesus wasn't the one in the water. It's like a head baker getting all the credit while the crew works the ovens.
Yes, baker. John 4:4 says, “Now He had to pass through Samaria.” Had to. That's the text's own word, and I'm not about to argue with it. Samaria is where this whole story happens.
Good guess, friend, but Moab never shows up in this story. Verse 4 says Jesus had to pass through Samaria. That's the stop where everything in this passage happens. Keep your eyes on the map.

Edom is a fine place name, friend, but it isn't in this passage. John 4:4 says, “Now He had to pass through Samaria.” That's the town-stop that sets up the whole conversation. I once guessed a recipe by the smell and baked the wrong thing for a whole afternoon, so I feel you.

That's the word, baker. John 4:6 says Jesus was “weary from His journey,” so He sat down by the well. Tired is something I understand after a full day of stamping. Nobody pressing cookies all day is skipping to the finish line.

Eager sounds like a fine word, friend, but it isn't the one the text uses. John 4:6 says Jesus was “weary from His journey.” That's why He sat down by the well. Eager folks usually don't sit down, so the text and the sitting go together.
The text doesn't say troubled, friend. It says Jesus was “weary from His journey,” and that's why He sat by Jacob's well. I'd call that a traveler who needs a seat. Weary is the word to hold onto.

That's it, baker. When the Samaritan woman comes to draw water, Jesus says to her, “Give Me a drink.” It's a short, plain request. Jesus speaks first, and that's what gets the whole conversation rolling.
That one's not in the text, friend. What Jesus says is “Give Me a drink.” The disciples are the ones who went into the town, to buy food (John 4:8). Jesus stays put by the well.
Jesus doesn't ask for her name in this passage, friend. He says, “Give Me a drink.” In fact, the woman is never named here at all. The first thing out of His mouth is a plain request for water.
Not quite, baker. John 4:8 says His disciples had gone into the town to buy food. So Jesus is sitting at the well without them when the woman arrives. He's talking one on one.
That's right, friend. John 4:8 says His disciples had gone into the town to buy food. So when the woman walks up, it's just Jesus at the well. Table for one, and a quiet well.

explanations.answer: Jews do not associate with Samaritans
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The text adds it in parentheses: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.” She says, “You are a Jew,” and she wonders how He can ask her, a Samaritan woman, for a drink. That's what has her so surprised.

explanations.answer: Men never come to draw at this well
explanations.explanation: The text never says that, friend. Her surprise comes from who is asking and who is being asked. John 4:9 says, “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.” A Jewish man is asking a Samaritan woman for a drink.

explanations.answer: She has no jar to draw water with
explanations.explanation: That's not her problem, friend. She came to draw water, and later she leaves her water jar behind (John 4:28). Her surprise in verse 9 is that a Jew is asking a Samaritan for a drink. The text explains it right there: “For Jews do not associate with Samaritans.”

explanations.answer: He has nothing to draw with
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. She says, “Sir, You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” She's looking at the facts: no bucket, deep well. I bet she was wondering how in the world He'd get any water at all.

explanations.answer: The well has gone completely dry
explanations.explanation: She never says it's dry, friend. Her words in John 4:11 are, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” A deep well with no bucket is a different problem than an empty one. Dry wells would be a whole other conversation.

explanations.answer: Samaritans are not allowed to share it
explanations.explanation: That's not her point, friend. She doesn't say anyone is forbidden from sharing. She says, “You have nothing to draw with and the well is deep.” Her trouble is the equipment, not the rules.

That's right, baker. In John 4:12 she asks, “Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well and drank from it himself, as did his sons and his livestock?” She's holding up a big name against a stranger sitting at the well. It's a bold question.

She does ask it, friend. John 4:12 has her saying, “Are You greater than our father Jacob, who gave us this well…?” She's comparing Jesus to the one who gave them the well. It's a big question from someone with a jar and a tired stranger in front of her.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst.” (John 4:14) No refills needed. That's the difference between this water and the well water.

explanations.answer: They will thirst once a year
explanations.explanation: That's a very specific schedule, friend, but it isn't in the text. Jesus says, “…whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst.” (John 4:14) Never is the word. Even my ovens need more checking than once a year.

explanations.answer: They will thirst a little less
explanations.explanation: A little less would be a nice discount, friend, but that's not what Jesus says. He says, “…whoever drinks the water I give him will never thirst.” (John 4:14) Never, not less. Hold onto that one.

explanations.answer: So she won't keep coming here to draw
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. She says, “Sir, give me this water so that I will not get thirsty and have to keep coming here to draw water.” (John 4:15) She wants to stop making the trip. I think anyone who has hauled water, or groceries, knows that feeling.

explanations.answer: So she can carry it to her whole town
explanations.explanation: That's not what she says here, friend. Her reason in John 4:15 is so she won't get thirsty and have to keep coming to draw water. She does go to the town later, but for a different reason. Here she's thinking about her own trips to the well.

explanations.answer: So she can give it to her livestock
explanations.explanation: Livestock do come up, friend, but in verse 12, when she mentions Jacob and his livestock. Her reason for asking is in verse 15: so she will not get thirsty and have to keep coming to draw water. That reason is about her own daily trip.
That's right, baker. She answers, “I have no husband.” Then Jesus tells her, “You are correct to say that you have no husband.” (John 4:17) Her answer is short and true.

explanations.answer: He is out in the fields
explanations.explanation: She doesn't give an excuse like that, friend. What she says is, “I have no husband.” Jesus tells her she's correct to say so (John 4:17). Short answer, no fields in sight.

explanations.answer: He is away on a journey
explanations.explanation: No journey in her answer, friend. She says, “I have no husband.” And Jesus replies, “You are correct to say that you have no husband.” (John 4:17) She kept it plain.
That's right, baker. She says, “Sir, I see that You are a prophet.” (John 4:19) Jesus told her about her five husbands, and now she's seeing Him differently. I'd say she's paying close attention.
Priest is a good job title, friend, but she doesn't use it. John 4:19 has her saying, “Sir, I see that You are a prophet.” A prophet is the word she lands on after what Jesus said about her husbands.
King is a big word, friend, but she doesn't say it here. She says, “Sir, I see that You are a prophet.” (John 4:19) That's the word she reaches for after hearing about her five husbands.

She has it flipped, friend, and that's easy to do. She says, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” (John 4:20) So the mountain goes with her fathers, and Jerusalem goes with the Jews. It's like mixing up the lids on two jars.

That's right, baker. She says, “Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, but you Jews say that the place where one must worship is in Jerusalem.” (John 4:20) The mountain and Jerusalem are the two places in question. The question is where to worship.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, “…a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” (John 4:21) She gave Him two choices, and He said neither. That's a plot twist.
That's her side's answer, friend, but not Jesus's. He says, “…a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” (John 4:21) Neither one gets the title.

That's the Jews' answer in her words, friend, but Jesus doesn't pick it here. He says, “…a time is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” (John 4:21) She offered two doors, and He pointed past both.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth…” (John 4:23) He also says, “God is Spirit, and His worshipers must worship Him in spirit and in truth.” (John 4:24) It's about how we worship, not where.

Gifts and fasting aren't in what Jesus says here, friend. He says the true worshipers will worship the Father “in spirit and in truth.” (John 4:23) Same line again in verse 24. Keep that phrase handy.
Silence isn't mentioned here, friend, and neither is being alone. Jesus says the true worshipers will worship the Father “in spirit and in truth.” (John 4:23) That's the phrase to remember.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him.” (John 4:23) The Father is the one doing the seeking. I think that's worth a smile.

The text says the opposite, friend. In John 4:23 Jesus says, “…the Father is seeking such as these to worship Him.” The Father is seeking true worshipers. Good news for anybody who wants to worship Him.

explanations.answer: I who speak to you am He
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus answers, “I who speak to you am He.” (John 4:26) She said the Messiah is coming, and He tells her the One speaking to her is He. A big moment at a well.

explanations.answer: He will come in many years
explanations.explanation: No waiting period in His answer, friend. Jesus says, “I who speak to you am He.” (John 4:26) She says the Messiah is coming, and He tells her that He is the One talking to her.

explanations.answer: You will meet Him in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Jerusalem isn't part of His answer, friend. Jesus says, “I who speak to you am He.” (John 4:26) No travel plans needed. She's already looking at Him.

Close, friend, but the text says otherwise. John 4:27 says the disciples were surprised He was speaking with a woman. But “…no one asked Him, ‘What do You want from her?’ or ‘Why are You talking with her?’” They kept it to themselves, and I think I'd have been staring too.

That's right, baker. John 4:27 says the disciples were surprised, “But no one asked Him, ‘What do You want from her?’ or ‘Why are You talking with her?’” They were surprised, but nobody said a word. Surprised and silent.

explanations.answer: Come see a man who told me everything I ever did
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. She tells the people, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” (John 4:29) She doesn't hold back. She goes back to the town, and she invites them to see for themselves.

explanations.answer: Come see a prophet who gave me living water
explanations.explanation: That's not what she says to the town, friend. In verse 19 she told Jesus she saw He was a prophet. But to the people she says, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” (John 4:29)

explanations.answer: Come see a teacher sitting by the old well
explanations.explanation: No teacher by the well in her words, friend. She says, “Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did. Could this be the Christ?” (John 4:29) It's about what He told her, and a question about who He is.
Not this crowd, friend. John 4:30 says, “So they left the town and made their way toward Jesus.” They didn't wait around. They went out to Him.
That's right, baker. John 4:30 says, “So they left the town and made their way toward Jesus.” They came out to Him. When a neighbor says come see, they came.

That's right, baker. The disciples ask one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?” (John 4:33) I think they were still stuck on the plain meaning of food. They had just come back with some from town.

explanations.answer: If He is planning to fast
explanations.explanation: Fasting never comes up, friend. The disciples ask one another, “Could someone have brought Him food?” (John 4:33) They're guessing He already ate.

explanations.answer: If He went into town alone
explanations.explanation: That's not their question, friend. The disciples were the ones who went into town (John 4:8). Their question is, “Could someone have brought Him food?” (John 4:33)

explanations.answer: To do the will of the One who sent Him and finish His work
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Jesus explains, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” (John 4:34) The disciples were thinking of a lunch. Jesus was talking about something bigger.

explanations.answer: To rest from His journey and then travel on to Galilee
explanations.explanation: Rest and a trip to Galilee aren't what He calls His food, friend. He says, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” (John 4:34) That's the answer, straight from His mouth.

explanations.answer: To teach in the synagogues and keep every Sabbath holy
explanations.explanation: That's a long list, friend, and none of it is in this verse. Jesus says, “My food is to do the will of Him who sent Me and to finish His work.” (John 4:34) His food is the will of the One who sent Him.
That's right, baker. Jesus says, “…lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.” (John 4:35) He says they were already ripe, no more waiting. Ripe fields, right now.

The text says the opposite, friend. In John 4:35 Jesus tells them, “…lift up your eyes and look at the fields, for they are ripe for harvest.” He contrasts it with their saying about four more months. The harvest is ready now.

explanations.answer: What they have not worked for
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Jesus says, “I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work, and now you have taken up their labor.” (John 4:38) Others did the hard work. The disciples get to step into it.
That's the reverse, friend. Jesus says, “I sent you to reap what you have not worked for; others have done the hard work…” (John 4:38) The disciples didn't do that work.

explanations.answer: What will not ripen for months
explanations.explanation: No waiting in this one, friend. Jesus said the fields were already ripe (John 4:35). And in verse 38 He says, “I sent you to reap what you have not worked for…” That harvest is ready.

That's right, baker. John 4:39 says many Samaritans believed in Jesus “because of the woman's testimony, ‘He told me everything I ever did.’” She told them what happened, and they believed. A simple story, passed along.
Prayers aren't in the verse, friend. John 4:39 says many believed because of the woman's testimony, “He told me everything I ever did.” Her testimony is what spread the word.
No gifts here, friend. The Samaritans believed “because of the woman's testimony, ‘He told me everything I ever did.’” (John 4:39) She didn't bring a present. She just told them what happened.
That's right, baker. John 4:40 says He stayed two days. They asked Him to stay, and He did. Two days with the people of that town.
A whole week is a long houseguest, friend, but the text says less. John 4:40 says, “…and He stayed two days.” That's the number.
Forty days is a lot of guest room, friend, and that's not what the text says. John 4:40 says He stayed two days. Two is the number to bake into your memory.

That's it, baker. They tell the woman, “…we have heard for ourselves, and we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” (John 4:42) They didn't stop at her words. They heard Him for themselves.
That's not the title they use, friend. They say, “…we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” (John 4:42) Notice they say of the world, not only for themselves.
Judge isn't what they say, friend. They tell the woman, “…we know that this man truly is the Savior of the world.” (John 4:42) That's a big thing to say after two days together.
